equation_request.abstract: In recent years, deep learning has had a profound impact on machine learning and artificial intelligence. At the same time, algorithms for quantum computers have been shown to efficiently solve some problems that are intractable on conventional, classical computers. We show that quantum computing not only reduces the time required to train a deep restricted Boltzmann machine, but also provides a richer and more comprehensive framework for deep learning than classical computing and leads to significant improvements in the optimization of the underlying objective function. Our quantum methods also permit efficient training of full Boltzmann machines and multi–layer, fully connected models and do not have well known classical counterparts.

specification.problem: Quantum-assisted training of (deep) restricted and full Boltzmann machines: use quantum computing to reduce training time and improve optimization of the underlying objective function, including models lacking efficient classical training.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Abstract-level reconstruction of the training objective and a standard background gradient; no quantum circuit details are given in the abstract, so only a small finite Boltzmann machine example is scoped.

equations.label: RBM energy
equations.latex: E(v,h)=-\sum_i b_i v_i-\sum_j d_j h_j-\sum_{i,j} W_{ij} v_i h_j
equations.description: Energy of a restricted Boltzmann machine configuration.
equations.justification: Standard RBM definition; the abstract names restricted Boltzmann machines but gives no formulas.

equations.label: Gibbs distribution
equations.description: Model distribution defined by the energy.
equations.justification: Standard definition needed to state the training objective.

equations.label: Likelihood gradient
equations.latex: \partial O_{ML}/\partial W_{ij}=\langle v_i h_j\rangle_{data}-\langle v_i h_j\rangle_{model}
equations.description: Gradient of average log-likelihood; the model expectation is the hard term quantum sampling would target.
equations.justification: Standard background for the optimization of the underlying objective function.

registers.name: vis
registers.role: visible units of the small example RBM

registers.name: hid
registers.role: hidden units of the small example RBM

registers.name: anc
registers.role: assumed ancilla for Gibbs-state preparation or amplitude/rotation encoding

specification.initial_state: Assumed: all registers in |0>; generic initial state, not given in the abstract.

steps.description: Assumed: apply Hadamards to vis and hid to create a uniform superposition over configurations (v,h).
Assumed: encode the energy E(v,h) in an ancilla via controlled rotations, with amplitude proportional to e^{-E/2}.
Assumed: post-select or amplitude-amplify to approximately prepare the Gibbs state with probabilities P(v,h), whose normalization is Z.
Assumed: use the prepared state to estimate the model expectation in the gradient; the data term is computed classically.

specification.measurement: Assumed: measure vis and hid in the computational basis after successful ancilla post-selection (ancilla=1), giving samples (v,h) from P(v,h). Repeat to estimate <v_i h_j>_model.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Assumed: average v_i h_j over samples for the model term, compute the data term classically from training data with sampled/conditional hidden units, form the gradient difference per eq_3, and update W (and b,d) by gradient ascent.
assumptions: Equations are standard background, not paper-specific.
